explanations.explanation: David, Israel's king, says, "I will bless the LORD at all times; His praise will always be on my lips." The title says this song comes from the time he pretended to be insane before Abimelech, the king who drove him away. Notice the song doesn't open with a complaint about that day. At all times means the LORD gets the song even then, and I'd have been tempted to write a strongly worded letter.

David doesn't say a word about praising the king. The king was Abimelech, and the title says he drove David away. The praise David promises goes somewhere else: "His praise will always be on my lips." Applauding the guy who just showed you the door would be a LOT to ask of any pair of lips.

Guarding his life isn't what David says here. He says, "I will bless the LORD at all times…" Later in the song he tells us the LORD delivered him from all his fears (Psalm 34:4). I think David's hands were too full of blessing to grab anything else.

David says, "let the oppressed hear and rejoice." The oppressed are people being pressed down, and he wants them to hear his boast in the LORD and be glad. A boast that lifts people up is the best kind to pass along.

Tremble isn't the word. David says, "let the oppressed hear and rejoice." He wants his boast in the LORD to land as good news for people being pressed down. Nobody needs shaking knees when the news is that good.
David doesn't say mourn. He says, "let the oppressed hear and rejoice." The oppressed are the very people he wants to hear about the LORD. I think he's hoping the news puts a smile on their faces.
The text says the opposite. David says, "Magnify the LORD with me; let us exalt His name together." He's inviting others in, and the word together is right there. A solo act doesn't need the word us.
That's right, it's false. David says, "Magnify the LORD with me; let us exalt His name together." He's not keeping it to himself. He's passing out invitations, and I'd have been first in line.

David says, "I sought the LORD, and He answered me; He delivered me from all my fears." Notice that the word is all. He doesn't say some of them or the small ones. That's David telling what happened when he sought the LORD.

This one is true. David says, "I sought the LORD, and He answered me; He delivered me from all my fears." Not just the little worries. All of them. I'd have double-checked that line, but there it is in black and white.

David says, "Those who look to Him are radiant with joy; their faces shall never be ashamed." Radiant means glowing, so you can see it on their faces. I think that's a better glow than anything an oven gives off.

It's the opposite of sorrow. David says those who look to the LORD "…are radiant with joy…" Their faces glow, and they "…shall never be ashamed." Looking to Him does something good to a person's whole face.

Worry doesn't make anybody radiant, friend. David says, "Those who look to Him are radiant with joy…" Then he adds that their faces "…shall never be ashamed." Looking to the LORD brings the glow, not the frown lines.
The text says more than that. David says the LORD "…saved him from all his troubles." The word is all, not just some. A partial rescue isn't what the verse describes.

It's false. David says, "This poor man called out, and the LORD heard him; He saved him from all his troubles." Not some of them, ALL of them. I was in a 25 cent bin and I'd take that deal in a heartbeat.

David says, "The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear Him, and he delivers them." Encamps means pitching a camp, like a guard setting up right around you. I think that's about as close as protection gets.

David doesn't say that. He says the angel of the LORD "…encamps around those who fear Him, and he delivers them." Nothing in the verse mentions rulers or nations. The camp goes up around the ones who fear the LORD.

Wealth isn't what David names. He says the angel "…encamps around those who fear Him…" Remember he called himself a poor man two verses back, and the LORD still heard him (Psalm 34:6). A full bank account isn't the ticket in this song.

David says, "Taste and see that the LORD is good; blessed is the man who takes refuge in Him!" Tasting is firsthand, not hearsay. You can't know what a fresh cookie is like by hearing about it, so I think David is inviting us to come find out for ourselves.

Mighty isn't the word David uses here. He says, "Taste and see that the LORD is good…" Then he adds, "blessed is the man who takes refuge in Him!" The invitation is to find out His goodness for yourself.
Hidden isn't the word David uses. He says, "Taste and see that the LORD is good…" Then he adds, "blessed is the man who takes refuge in Him!" The invitation is to taste and see that the LORD is good.

David says, "Fear the LORD, you His saints, for those who fear Him lack nothing." Nothing means nothing, friend. Saints are God's holy people, and David is talking to them directly. I have never once seen my pantry that full.
Courage isn't the word. David says, "…those who fear Him lack nothing." The word is nothing, which is bigger than any one thing on a list. He doesn't narrow it down to courage.

Wisdom is a good guess, but David doesn't name it. He says, "…for those who fear Him lack nothing." Nothing covers a lot more ground than wisdom alone. He's speaking to the LORD's saints, and the promise is that big.

David says, "Young lions go lacking and hungry, but those who seek the LORD lack no good thing." Young lions are strong hunters, and they still go without. The ones who seek the LORD lack no good thing. I think the point is that strength alone doesn't fill the plate.
That's not what David says. He says, "Young lions go lacking and hungry…" They may look strong, but they're the ones going without. The contrast comes right after, with those who seek the LORD.
David says no such thing about the lions. He says, "Young lions go lacking and hungry…" Nobody is crowning them. The ones who "…lack no good thing." are those who seek the LORD.

David asks who wants good days, and the first answer is "Keep your tongue from evil and your lips from deceitful speech." It starts with what comes out of your mouth. I'll be honest, I've said a few things to my own cookie dough that I'd take back.

David doesn't say that. For the one who wants good days, he says, "Keep your tongue from evil and your lips from deceitful speech." The first thing he points to is how we talk. Sorrow isn't on the list.

Feet aren't what David mentions first. He says, "Keep your tongue from evil and your lips from deceitful speech." The first step toward good days is about what we say. Then he moves on to turning away from evil and doing good (Psalm 34:14).
The text says the opposite. David says, "seek peace and pursue it." Seek and pursue are action words, not sitting words. Peace doesn't get delivered to the couch.
That's right, it's false. David says, "Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it." He gives us two verbs for one job, seek and pursue. I think that tells us peace is worth the chase.
David says, "The eyes of the LORD are on the righteous, and His ears are inclined to their cry." Inclined means leaning in to listen. The LORD isn't just looking, He's listening too.
Praise is a nice thought, but David says "…His ears are inclined to their cry." The righteous are crying out, and the LORD is leaning in to listen. That's the picture the verse gives.
Plans aren't what David says. He says, "…His ears are inclined to their cry." The LORD listens when the righteous cry out. Nobody has to hand Him a PowerPoint first.

David says, "…the face of the LORD is against those who do evil, to wipe out all memory of them from the earth." That's a heavy line, and it's good to say so plainly. It sits right beside the verse where the LORD's eyes are on the righteous (Psalm 34:15).
David says the opposite. The face of the LORD is against those who do evil, "…to wipe out all memory of them from the earth." It's a serious verse, and the memory doesn't get passed down.

Hidden for a time isn't what David says. He says the LORD's face is against those who do evil, "…to wipe out all memory of them from the earth." It's one of the heavier lines in this song. The word is wipe out, not hide.
David says, "The LORD is near to the brokenhearted; He saves the contrite in spirit." Near is a good word to hold onto. I think this verse is one to read slowly.
It's true. David says, "The LORD is near to the brokenhearted; He saves the contrite in spirit." The brokenhearted aren't off in the distance. Near means near.

The text says something different. David says, "Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the LORD delivers him from them all." The afflictions are real, and so is the deliverance. He never promises a trouble-free road, just a LORD who delivers.

That's right, it's false. David says, "Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the LORD delivers him from them all." Notice he says many, not none. And the word all shows up again, just like it did earlier in the song.
David says, "He protects all his bones; not one of them will be broken." That's a very specific kind of care. Every single bone, and not one is missed.
Counted isn't the word. David says, "He protects all his bones; not one of them will be broken." The care is in the protecting, so none of them break.
Hidden isn't what David says. He says, "He protects all his bones; not one of them will be broken." The verse is about protecting. Every one of those bones is kept from being broken.

David says, "Evil will slay the wicked, and the haters of the righteous will be condemned." That's a heavy line, and the word is condemned. Right after it, David says, "The LORD redeems His servants, and none who take refuge in Him will be condemned." (Psalm 34:22)
That's not what the verse says. David says, "…the haters of the righteous will be condemned." It's a serious verse. The word is condemned.
Scattered isn't David's word here. He says, "…the haters of the righteous will be condemned." It's a heavy verse, and the text uses the word condemned.

David ends with, "The LORD redeems His servants, and none who take refuge in Him will be condemned." Redeems is the word he closes on. The song ends with the LORD's servants and those who take refuge in Him.
Humbles isn't how David closes. He says, "The LORD redeems His servants…" Then he adds that "…none who take refuge in Him will be condemned." The last word of the song is a good one.

Tests is a fair guess, baker, but David doesn't close there. He says, "The LORD redeems His servants…" To redeem is to buy back and set free, and that's the LORD's work for His servants. Then David adds that "…none who take refuge in Him will be condemned." So the song ends with the LORD doing the rescuing, not putting His servants through a pop quiz.
